strengths: Substantial system contribution: TESSERA provides precomputed, global, annual, 10m-resolution 128-dimensional representation maps (2017-2024) with open-source code and model weights, a 'Model-as-Data' paradigm that genuinely lowers the barrier to entry for EO practitioners and is a valuable community resource.

Empirically strong and reasonably broad evaluation: on the INVEKOS crop benchmark, TESSERA+MLP consistently outperforms Random Forest and PRESTO across label regimes including one/few-shot (Fig. 2), and in canopy height estimation on Danum Valley it clearly beats both PRESTO (R2 0.66 vs 0.50) and four global/regional CHM products (Fig. 3), with spatially blocked cross-validation and multiple training runs.

Well-documented training methodology: the loss function (modified Barlow Twins with mix-up, Eqs. 8-12), temporal-sampling augmentations, global shuffle pipeline (Fig. 8, with empirical loss-stability evidence), and full pretraining hyperparameters are reported in enough detail to support reproducibility.

Honest reporting in places: the paper acknowledges that the BioMassters competition winner outperforms TESSERA in fully supervised settings and that cross-product comparisons are imperfect due to differing input sensors.

Diverse downstream coverage spanning classification, regression, segmentation, change/disturbance analysis, and an applied carbon-market use case, demonstrating transferability of the representations.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the approach is a fairly standard combination of dual Transformer encoders, Barlow Twins loss, an MLP fusion, and mix-up regularization borrowed from Bandara et al. [9]. The contribution is primarily engineering scale plus the released maps; no ablations are provided to justify the specific modifications (mix-up term, lambda values, 128-d embedding size, projector architecture), so the design choices are not empirically grounded.

Two of the five downstream evaluations are largely qualitative: burned-area detection (Sec. 2.4) rests on UMAP visualizations of just two 15x15 km regions with no quantitative metrics, no baselines (e.g., NBR differencing, existing BA algorithms), and no statistical support; the stocking-index comparison (Sec. 2.6) uses only 38 in-situ plots, and the per-product linear rescaling 'to minimize RMSE with respect to the in situ data' is fit on the same evaluation data, which weakens the comparison (Fig. 6 shows slope = 1.000 for TESSERA, consistent with fitting on the test set).

Geographic breadth of validation is narrow for the regression tasks: canopy height is evaluated on a single 5x6 km tropical site, so claims of superiority over global CHM products (which were designed for global coverage) should be tempered; AGB evaluation relies on a single benchmark region (Finland).

Missing or incomplete manuscript elements undermine polish and credibility: Section 2.1 and Section 2.2 substantially duplicate the crop-classification description; Section 2.6 contains an unresolved '(REF)' placeholder and an uncited 'Atzberger et al., 2025' reference; Fig. 5 caption misspells 'SpectralGBT' and Fig. 6 says 'conversation functions.' These suggest the paper was not fully assembled/proofread.

Baseline and fairness concerns: the flagship comparison is against PRESTO, a much smaller model trained on less data; stronger contemporary geospatial foundation models (e.g., Clay, DOFA, larger Prithvi variants) are either absent or included only in the segmentation experiment without reported numbers in the text. Also, pretraining used data spatially downsampled by a factor of 400 while inference/evaluation uses native 10m data; the train/inference resolution mismatch and its effect are not analyzed.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence: 'state-of-the-art across a diverse array of complex tasks' rests partly on qualitative analyses, and the conclusion generalizes from five tasks, two of which lack rigorous quantitative support. No uncertainty quantification for the canopy-height or AGB maps is provided despite the paper itself arguing that CHMs need 'quantified uncertainties.'

strengths: The 'Model-as-Data' paradigm — precomputing annual global 10m, 128-dimensional representation maps for 2017–2024 and releasing them openly — is a genuinely useful contribution that could substantially lower the barrier to entry for EO practitioners, and the large pretraining corpus (0.8B d-pixels from 3,012 MGRS tiles) is impressive in scale.

Evaluation spans five diverse downstream tasks (crop classification, canopy height, AGB, burned area, carbon-market stocking indices) covering classification, regression, and segmentation, with comparisons against both traditional baselines (RF) and foundation models (PRESTO, SpectralGPT).

The crop classification experiments are relatively thorough: multiple training-data regimes (1–30%), few-shot/one-shot settings, patch-based segmentation against several foundation models, and quantitative embedding-space metrics (Silhouette, Davies-Bouldin) beyond just visual UMAP inspection.

Engineering details supporting reproducibility are provided in the appendix: loss formulation (Eq. 8–12), training hyperparameters, GPU budget (~3,000 GPU hours on MI300X), and a custom global-shuffling data pipeline with an empirical demonstration of its effect on training stability (Fig. 8b).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the method is essentially Barlow Twins (Zbontar et al.) applied to pixel time series, explicitly building on Lisaius et al. [49], with a mix-up regularizer borrowed from Bandara et al. [9] and a standard dual-Transformer encoder architecture. No ablation studies are provided to justify any design choice (the mix-up term, GRU pooling vs. attention pooling, 40-timestep sampling, encoder depth, or the loss weighting λ_mix = 1.0), so the contribution is largely an engineering/data effort rather than a methodological advance.

The burned area evaluation (Section 2.4, Fig. 4) is purely qualitative — two subjectively discussed 15×15 km regions with UMAP scatter plots, no quantitative metrics (e.g., IoU/F1 vs. MTBS boundaries), no baselines, and no statistical support. Presenting this as one of the 'five diverse tasks' supporting the SOTA claim is not rigorous.

Evidence for generalization is thin in the canopy height task: validation is confined to a single 5×6 km tropical forest site (Danum Valley). The comparison against three global CHM products is arguably unfair since those models were not trained with local data, and only PRESTO provides a like-for-like foundation model comparison; no other temporal or SAR-fusion canopy height baselines are included.

Potential train/inference mismatch is unexamined: pretraining d-pixels are spatially downsampled by a factor of 400 from 10m data, while inference and downstream tasks use native 10m data. The impact of this domain shift on representation quality is neither analyzed nor ablated. Additionally, representations depend on random temporal sampling of 40 timesteps (with replacement if <40 valid dates), making the 'global representation map' product stochastic; averaging strategy and its effect are only mentioned in passing (Appendix A.9).
Section 1.2 states the fused representation is 'quantized' before the projector, but quantization is never defined, justified, or ablated — a material unexplained component in the core architecture.

The manuscript appears incomplete/under-polished: Section 2.6 contains a literal '(REF)' placeholder, cites 'Atzberger et al., 2025' outside the reference list, the VCM comparison relies on undisclosed linear rescaling details 'in the SI', and there are multiple typos ('SpectralGBT' in Fig. 5 caption, 'conversation functions' in Fig. 6 caption, 'Crop type classification inform vital'). These undermine confidence in the level of care taken.

The BioMassters/AGB comparison concedes that the satellite inputs differ between TESSERA and the benchmark models, and the bespoke winner still outperforms TESSERA at full labels; claims of robustness in low-label regimes rest on a single dataset with acknowledged incomparability.

Downstream baselines are narrow for a SOTA claim: the crop classification pixel task compares only RF and PRESTO, omitting stronger or more recent temporal foundation models (e.g., SatMAE, Prithvi, SpectralGPT) in the pixel-classification regime, and there is no fine-tuning comparison to test whether frozen representations genuinely outperform task-specific fine-tuned models.

strengths: Large-scale, practical contribution: TESSERA produces pre-computed global, annual, 10m, 128-dimensional representation maps (2017-2024) from fused Sentinel-1/Sentinel-2 time series, and the 'Model-as-Data' paradigm genuinely lowers the barrier for downstream EO users who cannot process raw imagery or train foundation models.

Broad and mostly convincing empirical evaluation across five diverse tasks (crop classification, canopy height, burned area, AGB, carbon-market stocking indices), with consistent gains over the closest foundation model baseline (PRESTO) and traditional baselines, particularly in low-label regimes (e.g., AGB RMSE on 1% labels beating SpectralGPT on 100%).

The canopy height experiment is methodologically careful: four-fold spatial cross-validation, 12 training runs, and comparisons against both foundation-model (PRESTO) and published global/regional CHM products, with sensible discussion of why global products fail in tall tropical canopy.

Substantial engineering and training detail in the appendix: full loss formulation (Barlow Twins + mix-up), 0.8B d-pixel pretraining corpus, global data-shuffling pipeline with empirical loss-stability evidence, and hardware/optimizer specifics, supporting reproducibility.
Claims of open-sourcing model, code, and representation maps, plus the privacy-preserving property of precomputed features, strengthen the societal usefulness of the work.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the approach is a fairly direct combination of dual-branch Transformers, Barlow Twins (explicitly building on Lisaius et al. [49]), and a mix-up regularizer from Bandara et al. [9]. The contribution is primarily scale and systems engineering rather than a new learning principle.

Missing ablations: there is no ablation of the mix-up term (L_MIX), the fusion strategy, embedding dimension, sequence length, the single-epoch training choice, or the sampling-with-replacement augmentation. Hyperparameters (lambda_BT = 5e-3, lambda_mix = 1.0) are reported without justification, so the sources of the performance gains are not isolated.

Uneven evaluation rigor: the burned-area section (2.4) is purely qualitative — UMAP plots on two 15x15 km regions with no quantitative metrics, no baseline comparison, and no held-out validation — yet the abstract and conclusion count it as one of the five benchmark tasks demonstrating SOTA performance.

Some baseline comparisons are not fully commensurate: global CHM products were never trained for the Danum Valley region (acknowledged by the authors, but still inflates the contrast); the AGB comparison to the BioMassters winner uses different input satellite data (also acknowledged); the VCM stocking-index comparison uses only 38 in-situ plots with linear rescaling fitted to minimize RMSE, which is a small and favorable evaluation design.

Manuscript incompleteness undermines polish and trust: a literal '(REF)' placeholder remains in Section 2.6, a broken cross-reference ('Appendix 5.1' instead of A.7.1), and a typo ('SpectralGBT' in Fig. 5 caption). The representation maps are only 'intended to be released publicly' with no repository link or persistence guarantee provided.

Statistical claims are under-specified: 'statistically significant advantages' and error bars 'over multiple runs' lack run counts, test definitions, and variance details in the main text for the crop experiments.

strengths: Large-scale, practically useful contribution: TESSERA produces analysis-ready 128-dim embeddings at 10 m resolution globally for 2024 (~250 TB released), with open model weights, training/inference code, and a PyPI library (GEOTESSERA). This 'embeddings-as-data' paradigm meaningfully lowers the barrier to downstream EO applications and is well-motivated (removing compositing's loss of temporal signal).

Broad empirical evaluation across five diverse downstream tasks (crop classification with pixel-wise and patch-wise segmentation, canopy height regression, AGB regression, burned-area detection, carbon-market stocking index), comparing against both task-specific baselines (RF, BioMassers winner, global CHM products) and other foundation models (PRESTO, GSE, SpectralGPT) with consistent favorable results, including strong label-efficiency behavior.

Solid methodological hygiene: four-fold spatial cross-validation for canopy height, multi-seed repetitions with error bars, RankMe-based ablations (Table 4) showing global data shuffling and mixup regularization are essential (F1 drops from 0.773 to 0.681/0.662 without them), and scaling-law analysis (Fig. 9) supporting design choices (projector dominates parameters, encoder relatively small).

Sensible adaptation of Barlow Twins to sparse, irregular EO time series: augmentations via independent temporal sub-sampling of cloud-masked observations rather than hand-crafted distortions, plus a mixup regularization term with a clearly specified loss (Eqs. 7-11). Quantization-aware training enabling ~4x storage reduction is a pragmatic and well-justified detail.

High reproducibility: detailed pretraining hyperparameters (Table 3), architecture breakdown (Table 2), data pipeline description including the global shuffle strategy with an empirical stability comparison (Fig. 8), and released code/data.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core components (dual Transformer encoders, Barlow Twins loss, projector scaling, mixup regularization) are standard, and the paper itself credits Lisaius et al. [95] for the key idea of Barlow Twins on cloud-corrupted EO series. The contribution is primarily systems/engineering scale rather than a new learning principle.

Uneven evaluation rigor across tasks. The burned-area detection task is essentially qualitative: evidence is UMAP visual inspection and an RF classifier trained on 2D UMAP projections (Appendix G.2), which is a nonstandard and questionable protocol; no quantitative comparison to established burned-area baselines (e.g., NBR-based methods) is provided. The stocking-index evaluation rests on only 38 in-situ plots, and comparison products are rescaled using the same data used for assessment.

Several evaluations are single-region, limiting evidence for the claimed global generality: canopy height in one 5x6 km Borneo site (R2=0.66), crop classification in Austria, AGB in Finland. The 'state-of-the-art' and 'outperforms in five diverse tasks' claims would be better supported by multi-region or multi-biome validation.

Baseline coverage is incomplete for some tasks: strong recent multimodal or time-series foundation models (e.g., Clay, Prithvi, Scale-MAE, DoFA) are catalogued in Table 5 but not empirically compared; GSE comparisons rely on annual embeddings whose spatial-context differences complicate attribution of gains to temporal modeling.

Comparison fairness caveats are acknowledged but not fully resolved, e.g., in the AGB task the benchmark models use different preprocessed satellite inputs than TESSERA, and the SpectralGPT comparison required substituting preprocessing from Pangaea.

Presentation is oriented toward a Nature-style format (supplementary note [1] 'Materials and methods are available as supplementary material', 'Competing interests' section) rather than CVPR conventions, and some claims ('unprecedented', 'transformative') are stronger than the evidence; the abstract contains typographical issues ('computation.,').

strengths: Substantial system-level contribution: TESSERA produces a global, annual, 10 m resolution, 128-dimensional embedding map (~250 TB for 2024), released openly with model weights, training/inference code, and the GEOTESSERA Python library, which materially lowers the barrier to applying EO embeddings for non-specialists.

Consistent quantitative wins on the tasks that are properly evaluated: pixel-wise crop classification (weighted/macro F1 across label-fraction regimes and one/few-shot settings), patch segmentation (mIOU/macro F1), canopy height at Danum Valley (R2 = 0.66, RMSE 8.88 m vs. negative or near-zero R2 for global CHM products and weaker FM baselines), and AGB on BioMastwers under low-label regimes.
Label-efficiency is convincingly demonstrated (e.g., AGB UNet on TESSERA at 1% labels beats SpectralGPT+UPerNet on full training data), which is a practically important claim for the field.

Reasonable supporting analyses: ablation study (Table 4) showing global shuffling and mixup are essential, RankMe embedding-quality metric, scaling-law analysis over projector depth/width and FLOPs, and quantization-aware training enabling a 4x storage reduction with negligible performance impact.
Generally well-documented methodology: pretraining hyperparameters, data pipeline, d-pixel representation, and downstream protocols are specified in sufficient detail to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the core method is a fairly direct application of Barlow Twins to pixel-level temporal sampling with a large projector, plus a mixup regularizer borrowed from prior work. The novelty is primarily in scale, data infrastructure, and the 'embeddings-as-data' delivery paradigm rather than in the learning algorithm itself.

Evaluation breadth is narrow relative to the generality claims: crop classification uses a single region (Austria, 2022), canopy height a single 5x6 km site (Danum Valley), and AGB a single benchmark (BioMastwers). Claims of 'state-of-the-art performance across a diverse array of tasks' and being 'transformative' rest on sparse geographic and task coverage.

The burned-area task (Section 2.4) is evaluated only qualitatively via UMAP visualizations of two 15x15 km California regions, with no quantitative metrics, no baseline comparison, and no statistical evidence; presenting this as one of five tasks benchmarked against SOTA overstates the evidence.

Baselines are incomplete and potentially cherry-picked: most comparisons are against PRESTO and GSE only. Recent strong FMs (e.g., Prithvi-EO-2.0, Anysat, DoFA, Galileo) are cited or mentioned in the segmentation setup but their results are not reported in the main comparisons. Statements like 'unprecedented in its ease of use, scale, and accuracy' are self-promotional given these gaps.

Some benchmark setups are not like-for-like: in the AGB task the authors acknowledge the satellite inputs used by baseline models differ from TESSERA's, and SpectralGPT required a re-implemented setup, weakening the strength of the 'outperforms' claims. Similarly, the stocking index comparison relies on linear rescaling of all products to the in-situ data, which conflates embedding quality with calibration procedure.

Several claims are not fully substantiated within the manuscript: the claimed global model performance/label-efficiency is validated mostly on European temperate and tropical-forest sites; robustness across biomes, urban areas, or the Global South (where the tool is most advertised) is not quantitatively tested; the UMAP clustering quality claims are not backed by the Silhouette/DBI metrics that the appendix defines but whose values are never reported.

Appendix Table 5's feature-by-feature comparison of ~80 foundation models is largely self-serving and of limited scientific value; several columns depend on subjective or unverifiable judgments ('potentially true').

Compression claim (factor of ~24x) is modest and the 96.7%-of-parameters projector is discarded at inference, making the 1.4B-parameter headline somewhat misleading about model capacity actually deployed.

strengths: Substantial and practical contribution: TESSERA delivers precomputed, 10 m, 128-d annual global embeddings (~250 TB for 2024) via an open GeoTESSERA library, model weights, and training/inference code, which genuinely lowers the barrier to entry for downstream EO applications and is a notable engineering and community contribution.

Broad empirical evaluation across five diverse downstream tasks (crop classification, canopy height, AGB, burned area, carbon-market stocking indices) with largely sensible baselines (RF, PRESTO, GSE, SpectralGPT+UPerNet, BioMassers winner, global CHM/AGB products), including label-efficiency regimes (1%–30% labels, one-shot/few-shot) and repeated runs with error bars.

Persuasive evidence of label- and compute-efficiency: e.g., surpassing the BioMassers competition winner's RMSE with ~1% of training labels (Fig. 4a), and outperforming both foundation-model and bespoke baselines with lightweight MLP/U-Net heads trained on frozen embeddings.

Useful diagnostics: ablation study (Table 4) isolating the importance of global data shuffling, mixup regularization, Sentinel-1 fusion, and quantization; scaling-law analysis over projector depth/width and FLOPs (Fig. 9); RankMe-based embedding richness analysis; UMAP cluster-quality analysis for crop classes.

Sound methodological motivation for the modified Barlow Twins objective: sparse temporal sub-sampling of cloud-affected series as a natural augmentation preserves phenological signal, avoiding lossy annual compositing—a reasonable and well-articulated design choice, supported by Fig. 1 and Appendix A.7.

High reproducibility: pretraining hyperparameters, data pipeline (global shuffle over ~800M d-pixels), and downstream protocols are documented in detail; datasets used are publicly available with one clearly flagged exception (Brazilian plot data under DTA).
Manuscript is well organized and clearly written, with detailed appendices covering architecture, loss function, and per-task methodologies.
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core method is a fairly direct application of Barlow Twins with temporal-subsampling augmentations, dual per-sensor encoders, and a large projector. The claim that TESSERA is 'unprecedented' (Sec. on contribution, Table 5) overstates the methodological advance; the novelty lies primarily in scale, the embeddings-as-data product, and system engineering rather than in the learning algorithm.

The burned-area evaluation (Sec. 2.4) is qualitative only—UMAP visualizations of two 15x15 km regions with no quantitative benchmark (no mIoU/F1/RMSE against MTBS references, no comparison to existing burned-area products or other foundation models), which weakens the 'state-of-the-art across five tasks' claim for this task.

Some baseline comparisons are not fully apples-to-apples and are acknowledged only briefly: the BioMassers comparison uses different satellite inputs than the benchmark winner/SpectralGPT (Sec. 2.3), and for the canopy-height global-product comparison the ALS acquisition (2020) temporally mismatches the products. For segmentation, patch-based models (Prithvi, Satlas) use finetuned encoders while TESSERA/PRESTO/GSE use frozen embeddings, complicating interpretation.

The ablation and scaling studies are conducted on a single task and region (Austrian crop classification), so conclusions about component importance (e.g., quantization having 'nearly no impact', Sentinel-1 contribution) may not generalize globally; the model's sensitivity to tropical/high-latitude regimes is not directly validated in the ablations.

Per-pixel, patch-independent embeddings deliberately discard spatial context at the encoder level; while the U-Net heads recover some spatial structure, the paper does not analyze failure modes where spatial context is essential (e.g., small objects, boundary precision), nor compare against spatially-aware state-of-the-art models on standard segmentation benchmarks.

Several strong claims (e.g., 'will prove transformative', 'state-of-the-art performance across a diverse array of tasks', Table 5 comparisons) would benefit from more hedging or direct head-to-head evidence; Table 5's qualitative checkmark survey of ~80 models is not independently verified.

Only one epoch of pretraining and compute-limited scaling are reported; while scaling trends are shown, the current model is clearly below the achievable frontier, and the practical effect on the released global product is not quantified beyond the five tasks.

Presentation issues: minor typos ('computation., ' in the abstract), occasional reliance on supplementary references for key methodology details, and the temporal mismatch between the 2024 embedding map and 2021–2022 downstream datasets is not always explicitly addressed.
